newsitem.title: USA: U.S. stalls on Afghan diplomat's takeover claim.
newsitem.headline: U.S. stalls on Afghan diplomat's takeover claim.

text.p: Afghanistan's two diplomats in Washington wrangled on Wednesday over which of them should represent their country, a U.S. official said.
"There was a question as to what flag should fly over the embassy, who was in charge," the official said, speaking on condition of anonymity.
By day's end, the old Afghan government's green, white and black flag was flying at the embassy and a temporary truce had been reached between the first and second secretaries, the official said.

A State Department spokesman said second secretary Seraj Jamal had declared that that he was authorised by Afghanistan's Taleban rulers to take control of the embassy and had asked first secretary and charge d'affaires Yar Mohammad Mohabbat to leave the building.

Jamal and Mohabbat are the only two diplomats in the Washington diplomatic list for the Afghan embassy which until now has represented the government of President Burhanuddin Rabbani, ousted from Kabul by Taleban last September.
"The State Department has not received any official communication which would verify Mr Jamal's assertion," spokesman John Dinger said. "If we do, we will address it."
"It is up to the Afghan foreign ministry in Kabul to inform us of any changes in the staffing of the embassy," Dinger told reporters.
"We are advising Mr Mohabbat and Mr Jamal to avoid any confrontation over this issue that might threaten either of the diplomats' status in the United States."
U.S. Secret Service and diplomatic security agents were dispatched on Wednesday to the Washington embassy, where a peaceful demonstration was held outside.

Because of the civil war in Afghanistan, the United States has maintained no diplomats in Kabul since the late 1980s and conducts its relations with the various Afghan factions through its embassy in Pakistan.

Taleban strengthened its claim to be the government of Aghanistan when it seized territory held by a rival group in the north of the country last weekend, although it lost control Wednesday of the key city of Mazar-i-Sharif.
The United States has evaded the issue of whether it is recognising a Taleban government by saying it recognises states, not governments.
"The issue of who staffs the Afghan embassy in Washington is a procedural one. It does not accord any sign of political approval by the United States government," Dinger said.
